newsitem.title: INDIA: Hope fades for missing fishermen in India cyclone.
newsitem.headline: Hope fades for missing fishermen in India cyclone.

text.p: Hopes are fading fast for more than 1,300 fishermen missing for five days after a deadly cyclone devastated India's southeast coast, the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh state said on Monday.
If fears prove correct, nearly 2,000 people are likely to have been killed by the onslaught of rains, 180 kmp (110 mph) winds and three-metre (10 foot) tidal waves, officials said.
"Their fate is not known. All of them could be dead," Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu told a press briefing, referring to the missing fishermen.
"Helicopters which flew over the Bay of Bengal could not locate them," he said. "The coastguard is searching for bodies."
Hundreds of corpses have already washed ashore.
Many fishermen set sail from tiny hamlets dotting Andra Pradesh's flat coastline only hours before the cyclone hit.

The more southerly Krishna district had been put on full cyclone alert, according to reports, but meteorologists say the cyclone changed tack in the last couple of hours and zeroed-in on the Godavari delta area.
Local fishing leaders disputed official statements that cyclone warnings were issued 24 hours ahead of the storm.

"The number 10 warning, indicating a severe cyclone, was sounded only hours before the storm hit the coast, by which time the fishermen had already been out at sea," said one fishing leader, Malladi Swamy.
Officials said some villages in the Amalapuram area, where an estimated 100,000 people lived, were still inaccessible.
But Andhra Pradesh government spokesman B.P. Acharaya said he did not expect the overall death toll to rise above 2,000. "It will be around 2,000 maximum," he told Reuters.
Tidal waves whipped up by the storm swept five km (three miles) inland, destroying houses, livestock and crops.
Many people were also killed by fierce winds which tore apart their flimsy houses and hurled uprooted coconut tree trunks through roofs.
Chief Minister Naidu appealed to international funding and aid agencies for help.
The calamity has caused losses estimated at 53.75 billion rupees ($1.5 billion) in damage to crops and property, he said.
Survivors in the fertile Godavari districts have complained that help did not come fast enough while officials in the state capital Hyderabad said relief and rescue workers were on a war-footing.
Officials said efforts were underway to prevent epidemics of waterborne diseases like cholera.
"Inoculation of a large number of people is on and well water is being chlorinated," state health minister Metla Satyanarayana said.
The stench of putrifying flesh from the bloated carcasses of dead cattle floating in the canals that criss-cross the Godavari river delta region filled the air close to camps and villages.
Dr Vijay Kumar at the Relief Control Room in Hyderabad said there had been no confirmed diseases reported but that the picture would become clearer in a few days.
There were close to 200,000 people huddled in the makeshift relief camps and more than 400 medical teams treating the sick and injured, officials said.
One of those seeking aid was Para Durga, a middle-aged woman with shrunken cheeks, who stood in line with a few ragged bundles of belongings.
"We have hardly eaten anything," she said.
